summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts handling domestic affairs. Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies here, so a visitor's legal position on those questions follows the Danish framework as received in Greenland.

The sources record no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No reported cases of prosecution under these provisions appear in the inventory.

Same-sex marriage has been in effect since 1 April 2016, adopted from a Danish bill passed unanimously on two occasions after the first lapsed through elections. It replaced the registered partnership regime that had run from 1 July 1996 until that date, and the bishop of the established church supported the change.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-determination basis. A law passed by decree in 2016 allows the sex designation on official identity documents to be changed without sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18, state that they want the change to their documentation, and observe a six-month reflection period before the request is confirmed. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

Parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics. The law establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

Public expression carries little risk on the record assembled here. Sources describe gay life as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with the first pride parade held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 attended by about 1,000 people and a modest annual march since. There is virtually no organised gay scene, attributed to the small and scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.
tangentialFactors:
The 1996 partnership law passed with virtually no public debate, and the 2016 marriage bill likewise drew no significant opposition recorded in these sources; the absence of contest over the reforms is itself an indicator of the political climate a visitor enters.

Public visibility is limited by demography rather than by prohibition. A population spread across a large territory with few urban centres means social venues concentrate in Nuuk, and the sources attribute the thin nightlife scene to those numbers rather than to legal constraint.

The territory's position inside the Realm of Denmark means most comparisons worth making run against the Danish framework: the marriage statute, the identity-document rules and the hate-speech provision are Danish instruments received locally, so a reading drawn from Denmark will usually be a fair guide, subject to the Greenlandic statute dates noted above.

The Greenlandic Broadcasting Corporation reported in August 2014 that a national association, LGBT Qaamaneq, had been founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working for political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters. Organised advocacy exists but operates at a scale consistent with the territory's population.
localsOnly:
Residents can lodge discrimination complaints with the Equal Treatment Board created by the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination of May 2024, in force 1 July 2024, whose prohibited grounds expressly include gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics. An Equality Council sits alongside the Board to promote non-discrimination.

The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights, giving residents an institutional route for human-rights advocacy separate from the complaints machinery.

LGBT Qaamaneq, founded in 2014, provides an organising point for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people and accepts supporters who are family, friends or colleagues.

Residents seeking to change the sex designation on identity documents apply under the 2016 self-determination law: no surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or diagnosis is required, but the applicant must be over 18 and complete a six-month reflection period before the change is confirmed. Greenlandic passports may be issued with an "X" descriptor.

Registered partnerships (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) were available from 1 July 1996 until the same-sex marriage law took effect on 1 April 2016, when the partnership law's application was repealed. Existing couples' positions on that transition are not addressed in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no reported prosecutions under Article 100 of the Criminal Code or under the hate-crime penalty enhancement, so their enforcement record is unresolved rather than established as unused.

Whether the "X" passport descriptor is accepted by foreign border authorities is not sourced here; the sources establish only that Greenlandic passports can be issued with it.

No source in the inventory addresses入境 or visa screening, entry refusals, or treatment of trans travellers by customs or immigration officials in Greenland, and none addresses access to transition-related healthcare for visitors.

The 2024 equal-treatment law took effect on 1 July 2024 and the sources give no case outcomes under it, so its practical operation is unverified.

No source documents violence against transgender people in Greenland, or the treatment of trans people in detention, policing or asylum procedures.
